I have farmed this land in Quzhou County my whole life. I am 63 years old now, and my husband and I manage about four mu of good flat land here on the North China Plain. We follow the double-cropping rotation that everyone in our village does — it is the only way to make full use of the land and feed our family.

The winter wheat is already in the ground, sown last October. I will manage it through to harvest in early June, then immediately plant summer maize on the same four mu. That is the system I trust, and it has always provided both grain for our own table and some income from selling the surplus.

For the wheat, I will apply top-dressing urea at the green-up stage in early spring — about 25 kg of nitrogen per mu. I already put down compound fertilizer as basal dressing in the autumn. I will irrigate three more times: once at green-up, once at jointing, and once at flowering. I spray herbicide once to control weeds, and I will spray insecticide and fungicide twice in total to protect against aphids and rust. I use an improved wheat variety, Jimai 22, which my neighbors also grow because it yields well and resists lodging.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I will plant Denghai 605 hybrid maize seed directly into the stubble with no tillage — that saves time, fuel, and labor, and the crop still grows well. I will apply compound fertilizer at sowing and top-dress with urea at the big trumpet stage, for a total of about 30 kg nitrogen per mu. I will irrigate twice: once at sowing if it is dry, and once at the tasseling stage. For pests, I spray herbicide once and insecticide twice to deal with corn borers and armyworms.

I do not plough for maize — no-tillage is what we have done for years, and rotary tillage is only for preparing the wheat seedbed in autumn. My yields are steady: I expect about 550 kg per mu of wheat and 600 kg per mu of maize.
